claim: Cnp-Cre::Pex5flox/flox mice lack peroxisomal protein import in Schwann cells
source: Cnp-Cre::Pex5flox/flox mice, termed cKO or 'mutants' in the following, lack peroxisomal protein import in Schwann cells (Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a showing experimental data

claim: The PNS of Cnp-Cre::Pex5flox/flox mice is well myelinated
source: The PNS of these mice is well myelinated and unlike the CNS (Kassmann et al., 2007) without immune-mediated injury, in agreement with pilot observations (Kassmann et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kassmann et al., 2007; Kassmann et al., 2011)

claim: Cnp-Cre::Pex5flox/flox mice show no immune-mediated injury in the PNS unlike the CNS
source: The PNS of these mice is well myelinated and unlike the CNS (Kassmann et al., 2007) without immune-mediated injury, in agreement with pilot observations (Kassmann et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to CNS pathology cited from Kassmann et al., 2007 and pilot observations from Kassmann et al., 2011

claim: About 50% genomic recombination was determined in mutant sciatic nerves, corresponding to the fraction of Schwann cell nuclei
source: Upon closer inspection, we determined about 50% genomic recombination, corresponding to the fraction of Schwann cell (SC) nuclei in sciatic nerves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: In mutant nerves, peroxisomes are import-deficient 'ghosts' with cytoplasmic catalase
source: In mutant nerves, these were import-deficient 'ghosts', as evidenced by cytoplasmic catalase, normally a luminal peroxisomal marker (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Peroxisomal products (PEO-) and plasmalogens (PEP-) are reduced in mutant nerves
source: Peroxisomal dysfunction in myelinating SC was confirmed by lipid mass spectrometry (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), showing reduced plasmalogens (PEP-) and its precursor alkylated phosphatidyl-ethanolamines (PEO-; Wanders, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipid mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, and cited knowledge from Wanders, 2014

claim: VLCFA are increased in mutant nerves, indicating accumulation of peroxisomal β-oxidation substrates
source: Also VLCFA were increased, indicating the accumulation of peroxisomal β-oxidation substrates (Figure 1d; Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d

claim: Nerve conduction velocity is diminished in mutants (28 ± 4.7 m/s) compared to controls (41.5 ± 3.6 m/s) at 2 months
source: Compound action potentials (CAPs) and NCV were diminished in mutants (mean: 28 ± 4.7 m/s) compared to controls (41.5 ± 3.6 m/s; Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Thresholds to evoke a signal were slightly elevated in mutants (155µA) versus controls (135µA)
source: Thresholds to evoke a signal were only slightly elevated (155µA versus 135µA), but the maximal response was 50% of control (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1f,g

claim: The maximal response in mutants was 50% of control
source: Thresholds to evoke a signal were only slightly elevated (155µA versus 135µA), but the maximal response was 50% of control (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1f,g

claim: In vivo recordings revealed significantly reduced compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) in mutant mice
source: Also, in vivo recordings revealed significantly reduced compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) in mutant mice (Kassmann et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kassmann et al., 2011

claim: CMAP reduction was more enhanced when stimulating proximally than distally, which clinically defines conduction blocks
source: This was more enhanced when stimulating proximally than distally, which clinically defines conduction blocks (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c and clinical knowledge about conduction blocks

claim: Structural myelin proteins including PMP22, MPZ/P0, and P2 were not significantly altered in mutant nerves
source: Surprisingly, by immunohistochemistry and Western blot analysis structural myelin proteins, including PMP22, MPZ/P0, and P2, were not significantly altered (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b

claim: PLP, a minor PNS myelin protein, showed significant reduction in mutant nerves
source: Only PLP, a minor PNS myelin protein, showed significant reduction.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b

claim: Myelin thickness, periodicity, and compaction were indistinguishable between mutant and control nerves by electron microscopy
source: Also by electron microscopy (EM), myelin thickness, periodicity, and compaction were indistinguishable (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 3c

claim: Internodal length was shorter in mutant (623 nm) than in control fibers (691 nm)
source: Next, we determined internodal length in teased fiber preparations, which was shorter in mutant (623 nm) than in control fibers (691 nm; Figure 1—figure supplement 3d), but unlikely sufficiently reduced to cause a slower conduction by itself (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by teased fiber data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d and cited knowledge from Wu et al., 2012

claim: The reduced internodal length is unlikely sufficiently reduced to cause slower conduction by itself
source: Next, we determined internodal length in teased fiber preparations, which was shorter in mutant (623 nm) than in control fibers (691 nm; Figure 1—figure supplement 3d), but unlikely sufficiently reduced to cause a slower conduction by itself (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and citation to Wu et al., 2012

claim: Axonal numbers and calibers were normal in mutant nerves at 2 months
source: Importantly, while the reduced CAP suggested significant axon loss at 2 months, the morphometric analysis of entire nerve cross-sections revealed normal axonal numbers and calibers (Figure 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric analysis data shown in Figure 1i

claim: Reduced CAPs were most likely caused by functional conduction blocks rather than physical axon loss
source: Thus, reduced CAPs were most likely caused by functional conduction blocks rather than physical axon loss.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that axon numbers are normal despite reduced CAPs

claim: Signs of axonal transport defects (APP accumulations) were not observed in mutant nerves
source: Signs of axonal transport defects (APP accumulations) were not observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e), and also, indirect signs of neurodegeneration (neuroinflammation) were not significantly enhanced in nerves at 2 months (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e

claim: Indirect signs of neurodegeneration (neuroinflammation) were not significantly enhanced in nerves at 2 months
source: Signs of axonal transport defects (APP accumulations) were not observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e), and also, indirect signs of neurodegeneration (neuroinflammation) were not significantly enhanced in nerves at 2 months (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a–d

claim: Neurofascin-155 (NF155) and axonal CASPR were normally localized in mutant nerves
source: Yet, both neurofascin-155 (NF155) and axonal CASPR, that is adhesion proteins that mediate axo-glial contacts (Desmazieres et al., 2014; Normand and Rasband, 2015), were normally localized (Figure 1j).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1j and cited knowledge from Desmazieres et al., 2014 and Normand and Rasband, 2015

claim: Detachment of paranodal loops was never found by EM, even where abnormally enlarged by accumulated vesicles
source: By EM, we never found the detachment of paranodal loops (Figure 1k,l), even where abnormally enlarged by accumulated vesicles (Kassmann et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1k,l and cited observation from Kassmann et al., 2011

claim: Nodal Nav1.6 and Kv7.2 were normally flanked by CASPR-positive paranodes in mutant nerves
source: Nodal Nav1.6 and Kv7.2, as well as their anchoring proteins, were normally flanked by CASPR-positive paranodes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c

claim: The juxtaparanodal potassium channel protein Kv1.1 displayed abnormal localization, frequently displaced into the adjacent internodal region, and to a minor extent into paranodes
source: Surprisingly, the juxtaparanodal potassium channel protein Kv1.1 displayed an abnormal localization, frequently displaced into the adjacent internodal region, and to a minor extent into paranodes.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,e

claim: Kv1.1 clusters were in the majority of cases still maintained at juxtaparanodes, suggesting that internodal mislocalization is secondary
source: Kv1.1 clusters were in the majority of cases still maintained at juxtaparanodes, suggesting that internodal mislocalization is secondary (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,e; Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,e and Figure 2a

claim: The pathology of internodal Kv1 channels progressively increased with age
source: Indeed, the pathology of internodal Kv1 channels progressively increased with age frequently presenting more than one extra cluster along one internode in aged mutants, while shifts into the nodal direction were not progressive (Figure 2a,b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e

claim: Shifts of Kv1 channels into the nodal direction were not progressive
source: Indeed, the pathology of internodal Kv1 channels progressively increased with age frequently presenting more than one extra cluster along one internode in aged mutants, while shifts into the nodal direction were not progressive (Figure 2a,b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e

claim: At 9 months, there was a twofold overall increase of Kv1.1 in nerve lysates
source: At 9 months, we determined a twofold overall increase of Kv1.1 in nerve lysates (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2c,d

claim: As most Kv1.1 is expressed by unmyelinated fibers, the increase of internodal Kv1.1 in myelinated axons may be significantly higher than the twofold overall increase
source: However, as most Kv1.1 is expressed by unmyelinated fibers, the increase of internodal Kv1.1 in myelinated axons may be significantly higher.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most Kv1.1 is in unmyelinated fibers

claim: Neuronal CASPR2 and TAG-1 on SC are essential for channel clustering at juxtaparanodes
source: Neuronal CASPR2, the cis-anchor for Kv1 channels in the axonal membrane, and TAG-1 on SC are essential for channel clustering at juxtaparanodes (Hivert et al., 2016; Poliak et al., 1999a; Savvaki et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hivert et al., 2016; Poliak et al., 1999a; Savvaki et al., 2010

claim: CASPR2 and TAG-1 colocalized with Kv1.1 at regular and ectopic internodal positions
source: Both proteins colocalized with Kv1.1 at regular and ectopic internodal positions (Figure 2e–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2e–g

claim: TAG-1 expression was slightly but not significantly elevated in mutant nerves
source: TAG-1 expression was slightly but not significantly elevated (Figure 2h).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2h

claim: Staining for myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG) did not reveal a connection between Schmidt-Lanterman incisures and the ectopic Kv1.1/TAG-1/CASPR2-positive clusters
source: In contrast, staining for myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG) did not reveal a connection between Schmidt-Lanterman incisures and the ectopic Kv1.1/TAG-1/CASPR2-positive clusters (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data (not shown)

claim: In mutant nerves entire membrane patches of the juxtaparanodal compartment accumulate, break-off, and drift into the internodal region
source: Although, we cannot exclude that enhanced expression of TAG-1 contributes to the formation of ectopic protein clusters, the observations suggest that in mutant nerves entire membrane patches of the juxtaparanodal compartment accumulate, break-off, and drift into the internodal region.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the colocalization data and the progressive nature of the pathology

claim: Many more gangliosides contained VLCFA in mutant nerve lysates (a 14-fold enrichment)
source: We analyzed sciatic nerve lysates from 9-month-old mutants by lipid mass spectrometry and noted that many more gangliosides contained VLCFA (a 14-fold enrichment; Figure 2h).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipid mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2i

claim: GM1 was restricted to paranodes in wild-type nerves but widely dispersed into the internodal myelin of mutant nerves
source: Also by immunostaining, GM1 was restricted to paranodes in wild-type nerves but widely dispersed into the internodal myelin of mutant nerves (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 2i).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2j

claim: Ganglioside GD1a could be immunostained as enlarged puncta (>5 µm) in internodal myelin of mutant nerves
source: Likewise, ganglioside GD1a could be immunostained as enlarged puncta (>5 µm) in internodal myelin of mutant nerves (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a

claim: GD1a-containing vesicles that colocalized with LAMP1 were a frequent finding in mutant internodes, but rarely observed in controls
source: These GD1a-containing vesicles that colocalized with LAMP1 were a frequent finding in mutant internodes, but rarely observed in controls (Figure 3a, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Paranodal loops in conditional mutants showed vesicular inclusions of variable size and electron-density
source: Paranodal loops in conditional mutants showed vesicular inclusions of variable size and electron-density (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3b

claim: The majority of vesicular inclusions in paranodal loops were LAMP1-positive
source: By immune-labeling of ultra-thin cryosections and teased fibers, the majority of these were LAMP1-positive (Figure 3c,d; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immuno-electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3c,d

claim: Lysosomal LIMP-2 marked small puncta in controls (<500 nm), but giant compartments within mutant paranodes
source: Even more striking, lysosomal LIMP-2 marked small puncta in controls (<500 nm), but giant compartments within mutant paranodes (Figure 3e, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3e

claim: Strongly increased abundance of LAMP1 and LIMP-2 was confirmed by Western blotting
source: Strongly increased abundance of LAMP1 and LIMP-2 was confirmed by Western blotting (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3f,g

claim: Decreased mRNA levels of LAMP1 and LIMP-2 suggest that the enrichment marks organelle accumulation rather than enhanced lysosomal biogenesis
source: Decreased mRNA levels (Figure 3h) suggest that the enrichment of LAMP1 and LIMP-2 marks organelle accumulation rather than enhanced lysosomal biogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3h

claim: Neither EEA1, RAB7, nor ATG5 markers were increased at mutant paranodes
source: We thus phenotyped accumulated vesicles with antibodies specific for EEA1, RAB7, and ATG5. Neither marker was increased at mutant paranodes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c

claim: The majority of accumulating vesicles within mutant paranodes are likely bona fide lysosomes
source: Therefore, the majority of accumulating vesicles within mutant paranodes are likely bona fide lysosomes, serving the degradation of myelin-associated proteins/lipids, including gangliosides (Luzio et al., 2007; Saftig and Klumperman, 2009).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of other organelle markers and cited knowledge from Luzio et al., 2007 and Saftig and Klumperman, 2009

claim: Paranodal lysosomes and peroxisomes show a close spatial association
source: To determine the relationship between paranodal lysosomes (Gatzinsky et al., 1997) and peroxisomes, we immunostained for PMP70 and LAMP1, revealing a close spatial association (Figure 3i) as reported for cultured cells (Chu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3i and cited observation from Chu et al., 2015

claim: Higher activities of lysosomal α-mannosidase and β-hexosaminidase were determined in mutant nerve lysates
source: We determined higher activities of lysosomal α-mannosidase and β-hexosaminidase in mutant nerve lysates (Figure 3j), and note that increased compartment size and enzymatic activities are known phenomena of lysosomal disorders (Sardiello and Ballabio, 2009), yet associated with organelle dysfunction.
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3j and cited knowledge from Sardiello and Ballabio, 2009

claim: Cnp-Cre::Hsd17b4flox/flox mice (MFP2 conditional knockout mice) share the key features of the phenotype, including ectopic internodal Kv1.1 clusters
source: However, we found that Cnp-Cre::Hsd17b4flox/flox mice (referred to as MFP2 conditional knockout mice in the following), which specifically lack peroxisomal β-oxidation (Verheijden et al., 2013), share the key features of this novel phenotype, including ectopic internodal Kv1.1 clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–e), confirming the important role for glial lipid metabolism in maintaining axonal membrane composition, and function.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–e and cited knowledge from Verheijden et al., 2013

claim: Sciatic nerve axons and myelin were morphologically intact in ABCD1-deficient mice, even at 22 months of age
source: Sciatic nerve axons and myelin were morphologically intact, even at 22 months of age (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 4a–c

claim: ABCD1-mutants exhibited a similar mislocalization of Kv1.1 positive channels as observed in both conditional (Pex5 and Mfp2) mutants
source: However, ABCD1-mutants exhibited a similar mislocalization of Kv1.1 positive channels as observed in both conditional (Pex5 and Mfp2) mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4d–e

claim: Mislocalization of internodal Kv1.1 was temporally progressive in ABCD1-mutants
source: The quantification showed that mislocalization of internodal Kv1.1 was temporally progressive.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Significant alterations in Kv1.1 localization were observed only at 22 months of age in ABCD1-mutants, but not yet at 2 months
source: In accordance with our model of membrane patches drifting into internodes, significant alterations were observed only at 22 months of age, but not yet at 2 months (Figure 4d–e).

claim: The Kv1.1 pathology in ABCD1-mutants was accompanied by lysosomal accumulates in myelinated fibers
source: This pathology was accompanied by lysosomal accumulates in myelinated fibers (Figure 4f–h).

claim: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids important for stabilizing membrane-spanning proteins and axon-glia interactions
source: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids important for stabilizing membrane-spanning proteins and axon-glia interactions (Susuki et al., 2007).

claim: Gangliosides are frequently esterified with VLCFA and 2-hydroxy fatty acids
source: For example, gangliosides, which are frequently esterified with VLCFA and 2-hydroxy fatty acids (Chrast et al., 2011; Sandhir et al., 2000), must be degraded in lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chrast et al., 2011 and Sandhir et al., 2000

claim: Gangliosides must be degraded in lysosomes
source: For example, gangliosides, which are frequently esterified with VLCFA and 2-hydroxy fatty acids (Chrast et al., 2011; Sandhir et al., 2000), must be degraded in lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ganglioside metabolism

claim: Subsequent β-oxidation of VLCFA and 2-hydroxy fatty acids requires peroxisomes
source: However, subsequent β-oxidation of VLCFA and 2-hydroxy fatty acids requires peroxisomes (Foulon et al., 2005; Wanders, 2014).

claim: The mouse model provides first in vivo evidence for functional interactions between lysosomes and peroxisomes
source: Thus, our mouse model provides first in vivo evidence for functional interactions between lysosomes and peroxisomes, so far only discussed for cultured cells (Chu et al., 2015).

claim: One consequence of lysosomal impairment is the perturbation of normal ganglioside turnover

claim: Gangliosides are in close association with Kv1-anchoring proteins
source: Gangliosides are in close association with Kv1-anchoring proteins (Loberto et al., 2003) and provide stability to the juxtaparanodal clusters (Susuki et al., 2007), which resemble giant membrane 'lipid rafts'.

claim: Gangliosides provide stability to the juxtaparanodal clusters

claim: Juxtaparanodal clusters resemble giant membrane 'lipid rafts'
source: Gangliosides are in close association with Kv1-anchoring proteins (Loberto et al., 2003) and provide stability to the juxtaparanodal clusters (Susuki et al., 2007), which resemble giant membrane 'lipid rafts'.

claim: Lack of ganglioside breakdown causes their accumulation in the glial juxtaparanodal membrane
source: As mechanism for ectopic localization of axonal Kv1 channels, we suggest the following working model (Figure 4—figure supplement 2): Lack of ganglioside breakdown causes their accumulation in the glial juxtaparanodal membrane.

claim: Accumulated gangliosides cause clusters of Kv1 and associated anchoring proteins to gain abnormal stability, break-off, diffuse into the internodal region, and escape from regular turnover

claim: Glial TAG-1 likely remains anchored to the axonal Kv1-/CASPR2-/TAG-1 clusters

source: Kv1-channels are fast-opening, voltage-gated channels that are activated by mild voltage-shifts and thought to regulate fiber excitability (Glasscock et al., 2012).

claim: The integrity of Kv1 channels is impaired in CASPR2-/- mice, but perturbation of nerve function is not a feature
source: The integrity of Kv1 channels is also impaired in CASPR2-/- mice, but perturbation of nerve function is not a feature (Poliak et al., 2003).

claim: Unlike PEX5 mutant nerves, CASPR2-/- nerves do not exhibit elevated levels of Kv1.1 channel protein
source: Unlike PEX5 mutant nerves, CASPR2-/- nerves do not exhibit elevated levels of Kv1.1 channel protein.

claim: The ectopic Kv1.1+ clusters are situated directly adjacent to juxtaparanodes in CASPR2-deficient fibers, not along the internodes as observed in PEX5 mutants
source: Also, the ectopic Kv1.1+ clusters are situated directly adjacent to juxtaparanodes in CASPR2-deficient fibers, not along the internodes as observed in PEX5 mutants.

source: Considering the severe progressive decline of nerve function in PEX5 mutant mice, which becomes clearly more affected with age (data not shown), it is unlikely that a rather non-progressive pathology, that is the shift of Kv1 into paranodes, is the underlying cause of conduction slowing.

claim: The progressive shift of Kv1 toward internodes correlates well with disease progression
